analysis.investment_thesis: Infonative Solutions fails the Magic Formula's critical "good business" test — a 0.45% ROE indicates the company earns essentially nothing on its capital, which no earnings yield can compensate for. A cheap-looking P/E of 7.96 on a 30 Cr micro-cap with negligible profitability is a value trap, not a bargain.
key_strengths: Low headline P/E of 7.96 suggests surface-level cheapness
Operates in asset-light custom learning/IT services (potentially low capital needs)
key_risks: ROE of 0.45% implies ROIC is catastrophically below the >20% Magic Formula threshold
Tiny 30 Cr market cap with 0.04% FII / 0% DII = illiquid, no institutional validation
Recent 2024 listing + 2014 incorporation = limited track record of sustained returns
red_flags: ROE <1% — the business generates virtually no economic return on capital
P/E may be distorted by one-off IPO-period earnings given SME-listed status
Zero DII ownership suggests no quality institution has validated this name
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies on two axes: earnings yield (cheapness) and return on capital (business quality). Infonative fails decisively on the second axis. A 0.45% ROE — even after assuming modest leverage — implies ROIC in low single digits, orders of magnitude below the >20% bar that makes a business worth owning. The whole point of the Magic Formula is to buy good businesses cheaply; a mediocre business at any price is still mediocre, and compounding at near-zero destroys value over time relative to a risk-free alternative.

The apparent 7.96 P/E and resulting ~12.5% earnings yield look attractive in isolation, but SME/micro-cap IPOs frequently show inflated trailing earnings from the listing period that don't persist. With a 30 Cr market cap, 0% DII ownership, and a custom e-learning niche with low barriers to entry, there is no identifiable moat to sustain returns even if profitability improved. This is a clear avoid — it's cheap-looking but not good, which is exactly the combination the Magic Formula is designed to filter out.
